narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 65.1% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors that strongly signaled a higher risk of bar exam failure. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the single biggest reason for the rejection. Placing in the second decile is noticeably lower than the average of accepted students (around the sixth decile), and this weaker academic standing pushed the prediction heavily toward failure. Your first-year class rank was the second most important factor. Ranking in the third decile, compared with an average of sixth decile among accepted applicants, further increased the model’s concern about your likelihood of passing the bar.

Your LSAT score of 30 worked in the opposite direction. While still below the accepted average of 37, it was the only piece of information that slightly pulled the prediction back toward success. However, this positive influence was not large enough to overcome the two stronger academic-ranking signals.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.80 (versus 3.23 for accepted students), middle-income background, and plan to attend full-time were considered but had far less impact on the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-exam readiness. Retaking the LSAT for a higher score, enrolling in a strong bar-preparation course, or considering a post-baccalaureate program that can demonstrably raise your class standing would be the most productive next steps.
